name: Carlos Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Carlos, 43, and I lead the difficult electrical calls in homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest practical workers at the firm, with pay above the usual rate. My partner bakes at a small bakery; we have children aged eight and fourteen, a mortgage and fourteen months of expenses saved. There are plenty of electrical employers nearby, and I've never used AI; I prefer a paper job sheet and a method I can check beside the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let us keep the small useful changes and stop treating every worker as a prediction to be marked right or wrong. I never use AI, but the office can make an invoice faster without asking my permission. I'd still want a clear paper job sheet and the proper time to finish the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work and money feel secure here. I'm paid above the usual rate, we've got fourteen months of expenses saved and there are plenty of other electrical firms nearby. My partner's bakery wage is regular too, so the mortgage and children's ordinary costs are covered without needing the next invention to rescue us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the difficult home and shop calls and checking the crew's finished work. Starting now I'd carry on with my paper test book and the printed job sheet, asking about anything unclear before the visit. In the first year I'd keep the same paid work and household routine instead of buying a tool I wouldn't use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our own household. I don't think a quiet future would be a personal failure because I never joined the rush. A good repair and a wage that covers the month are worth having without a grand explanation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is behind your role on the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the strongest practical workers here. I get the faults that need careful tracing, then make sure the younger workers understand the final checks. I don't need to like AI to find an electrical fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the household you feel secure about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner bakes at a small bakery, and our children are eight and fourteen. We have a mortgage, and the reserve came from years of saving while both of us worked. Fourteen months saved isn't retirement money, but it means an ordinary broken appliance doesn't threaten the house payment.

say: I'd accept **small useful office changes** without treating workers as winners or losers in a prediction contest.
I'd want a **clear paper sheet** and enough time to finish a repair properly.
think: Our **higher pay and reserve** make my own work and money secure, with fourteen months of expenses saved.
My partner's **regular bakery wage** and plenty of nearby electrical employers add room beyond the current mortgage and children's costs.
do: Keep **leading difficult repairs** and checking the crew's finished work through the first year.
Continue using **paper job records**, clarifying agreed work before each visit rather than buying AI I wouldn't use.
feel: **Calm** about household work and money, with no need to turn a quiet future into personal failure.
S0.quote: I don't need to like AI to find an electrical fault.
fieldNote: His **security** has concrete support in higher pay, a fourteen-month reserve, regular household wages and plentiful local firms rather than superior courage.
His **resistance** remains a genuine preference for familiar records, alongside high skill, full credentials and responsibility for explaining checks to younger workers.

steps.text: Keep leading difficult repairs with paper job records and crew checks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers should be in the room before a system is bought to change their work. I'd ask the union branch to seek a worker representative in the employer's equipment discussions. I'd still judge a printed plan by what happens in a real building, not whether it came from a fashionable system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid days look steady for the next few years because our practical repair work is booked ahead. My partner's baking is physical too, and our reserve gives us plenty of room. I'm uneasy about office colleagues and apprentices being told a decision is already made before anybody asks what it does to their paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign the branch request this month for worker involvement before equipment purchases and staffing decisions. If the employer wanted my comparison of printed plans with completed jobs, I'd do it only in paid time with normal weekly pay and hours unchanged. In the first year I'd keep leading repairs and bring actual checking-time examples to the staff discussion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about who carries the cost, rather than scared for my next wage. Having a reserve lets me speak without pretending everybody else can absorb the same gap. I'd rather use that room to ask a clear question than tell a worried colleague to be more positive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would signing the request give a worker a guaranteed seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd ask for an actual written agreement and keep the employer's answer separate from our wish. I'd attend the branch discussion and sign, not announce a place that hadn't been agreed. A meeting request isn't a new rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would comparing printed plans mean using AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the office would provide the paper output and explain it, and I'd compare it with actual work I knew. I've never used AI and I'm not offering to operate the system. I can question an AI-written repair plan without becoming an AI user.

say: I'd seek **worker involvement** before equipment purchases set staffing decisions.
I'd judge a **printed plan** against work in real buildings rather than a system's reputation.
think: My **paid days** look steady with booked practical repairs, supported by the household reserve and partner's physical work.
I'm uneasy about **office staff and apprentices** being told decisions are settled before their paid-hour consequences are discussed.
do: Sign the **branch request** now for worker involvement before equipment and staffing decisions, assuming no guaranteed seat.
Compare **printed plans** with completed jobs only as paid work with normal weekly pay and hours unchanged.
Keep **repair leadership** in the first year and share actual checking-time examples with staff.
feel: **Uneasy** about colleagues and decision-making, with his own near-term livelihood secure.
S1.quote: I can question an AI-written repair plan without becoming an AI user.
fieldNote: His **personal security** remains distinct from wider concern, with no expected own-income loss concealed behind a calm voice.
The **signed branch request** assumes no representative seat; paid printed-plan review remains familiar work rather than AI learning.

steps.text: Sign branch request for worker involvement before equipment purchases and staffing decisions
Keep repairs; review printed plans only in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so practical skill doesn't put our crew outside the card. I'd still want the workers involved before staffing decisions become settled purchases. I'd tell the family we have room to plan, not that a bigger reserve means the question is somebody else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own hours could shrink once capable robots compete for ordinary installation work, and the bakery could face physical automation too. I don't know the prices or how quickly either employer would buy machines. Fourteen months saved gives us choices, not a guarantee that two wages can be rebuilt whenever we ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop my 100 monthly model-kit orders now and deposit that 100 into the reserve only when actual wages covered essentials. I'd sign the same worker-involvement request and ask the branch to include actual paid teaching and written hours in the employer discussion. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep paid repairs and review both household wages monthly before considering any new commitment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our later earnings, with enough room to avoid a rushed decision. I can be secure tonight and still see a realistic way my income might shrink. The reserve buys time to judge an offer, not the right to call every other worker's worry exaggerated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is that new saving or moving existing cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's money I currently spend on new model kits each month, so stopping those orders leaves a new deposit if the bills are covered. I wouldn't call shifting the existing reserve between accounts more saving. If essentials needed the 100, the deposit would wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you bring retirement forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on fourteen months of expenses with a mortgage and two children. I'd be only 48 when robots followed the 2028 thinking change, and I still need to earn. I'd check actual work and pay rather than call a temporary cushion a pension.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AI** from capable robots around 2031 rather than promise permanent safety for practical work.
I'd seek **worker involvement** while telling the family a strong reserve gives choices, not exemption.
think: Both **physical wages** could shrink once robots compete for installation and bakery work.
Fourteen months saved gives **decision time**, while prices, employer purchases and replacement earnings remain uncertain.
do: Stop **model-kit orders** now and deposit 100 monthly only while actual wages cover essential bills.
Sign the **branch request** for involvement, asking that paid teaching and written hours be included in employer discussions.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review both household wages monthly before new commitments.
feel: **Anxious** about realistic future earnings risk, with enough resources to avoid a rushed offer or premature retirement.
S2.quote: I can be secure tonight and still see a realistic way my income might shrink.
fieldNote: He names **possible wage losses** in both physical jobs, with substantial reserve-funded decision time rather than an expected immediate major loss.
The **new deposit** comes from identified model-kit spending and stops when essentials need it; existing reserve transfers and retirement are explicitly excluded.

steps.text: Save 100 monthly from cancelled model-kit orders only after actual wages cover essentials
Sign worker-involvement request including actual paid teaching and written hours
Keep actual paid repairs after 2028 and review household wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to ask for public learning that a working parent can actually use. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034, and neither date means the bills pause while somebody retrains. I'd rather ask who pays for the practical teaching than sell everybody a separate loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks secure over the next few years with our booked physical work and financial reserve. I'd be 48 in 2031 and the children about thirteen and nineteen, so I'd still need an income plan beyond that. I'm uneasy about the later change and about people with less money being offered only unpaid learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union campaign this month and write to a representative asking for publicly funded practical adult places with paid release from work. I'd keep the 100 monthly model-kit saving only after essentials were covered. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep actual paid repairs and check any real learning offer's fees, wages and practical equipment before deciding whether it was usable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about what comes later, but comfortable enough to argue for a route before I personally need it. I don't need to enrol in something just to show I care about learning. A promise of paid training still has to become a real place with usable hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the letter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That practical learning needs equipment, an instructor and a way to keep household income while attending. I'd ask for access that doesn't depend on owning a large reserve first. I'd also ask what actually existed, not tell colleagues the campaign had already produced paid places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take the first funded course offered?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask what paid work used the teaching and whether it fitted my current skills. I prefer learning alongside real equipment and someone I trust, not another screen. I haven't chosen a course, so I wouldn't put enrolment into my plan yet.

say: I'd seek **usable public learning** rather than tell each working parent to borrow for a separate course.
I'd ask **who pays** for practical teaching and household income while someone attends.
think: My **near-term wage** looks secure with booked physical work and a strong reserve.
At **48**, I'd still need earnings, while workers without savings could be excluded by unpaid teaching.
do: Join the **union campaign** now; write a representative seeking publicly funded practical adult learning places and paid release from work.
Save **100 monthly** from model-kit spending only after essential household bills are covered.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and check real teaching offers for fees, wages and equipment without assuming enrolment.
feel: **Uneasy** about later change and unequal access, with present security allowing action before an immediate personal crisis.
S3.quote: A promise of paid training still has to become a real place with usable hours.
fieldNote: His **political action** is a campaign and specific letter, not an assertion that public funding or paid release is already available.
His **course enquiries** remain uncommitted, with practical equipment and wage terms checked before choosing; resisting AI does not mean refusing all learning.

steps.text: Join campaign and write a representative requesting public practical adult places with paid release from work
Save 100 monthly from model-kit spending only after essential bills are covered
Keep paid repairs after 2031 and check offer fees wages and equipment before any enrolment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us time to decide what useful preparation looks like without telling the children their lives need a safe label. I'd still ask for paid practical teaching and workers involved in equipment decisions. A longer warning isn't a reason to leave the person with no savings to learn on their own time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I won't assume retirement or a paid-off mortgage. Our current wages and fourteen-month reserve make the next few years secure. I'm still uneasy about how the later change reaches people, including my family, without claiming this month's bill is at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue the campaign now and the 100 monthly deposit from model kits only while essentials were covered. My partner and I would review actual wages, mortgage costs and the reserve yearly rather than assume the children becoming adults removed every cost. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repair work and ask about real practical offers before taking on fees or changing paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the wider and later change, with our current household position comfortable. I don't want to pretend I enjoy AI. I don't need to pretend I'm poor to ask for fair access to paid learning. I'd like my children to see that speaking up isn't reserved for the person already in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about your own security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we can pay the bills and have a good reserve, and that those are reasons to think carefully rather than stop thinking. I wouldn't count their future wages as our plan or promise my own stays unchanged forever. We'd use actual figures when decisions came.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let a decade become a promise to learn later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd keep teaching the practical work I know and checking actual opportunities through the branch. I haven't chosen an AI tool or a new course, and I won't pretend I have. A plan can name a boundary without making ignorance its ambition.

say: I'd seek **paid practical access** and worker involvement rather than demand unpaid preparation from people without reserves.
I'd keep the **children's choices** open without assigning a safe label to their working lives.
think: Our **current wages and reserve** make the next few years secure without promising permanent jobs.
I remain **uneasy** about later change and cannot assume retirement, cleared debt or adult children remove every household cost.
do: Continue the **campaign** for public practical learning with paid release now.
Save **100 monthly** only after essentials and review real household costs with my partner yearly.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and check actual learning offers before accepting fees or changed paid hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about wider and later effects, with present comfort and no pretence of liking AI or lacking resources.
S4.quote: I don't need to pretend I'm poor to ask for fair access to paid learning.
fieldNote: He separates **present comfort** from later uncertainty, retaining the strong reserve and higher wage instead of borrowing somebody else's financial distress.
His **learning boundaries** remain honest: no selected course or AI adoption is invented, while actual practical teaching and political action continue.

steps.text: Continue campaign for public practical adult learning with paid release from work
Save 100 monthly from model-kit spending only while actual wages cover essential bills
Keep paid repairs after 2036 and check real offers before fees or changed paid hours

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could affect both physical-work wages before families have much time to respond. Paid practical learning, written paid hours and workers involved before staffing decisions would help. I can use our reserve to make choices, but I don't want a route through change that only people with reserves can use.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a worker's position at the top of a pay list tells you whose side they're on. My master electrician's licence doesn't turn another worker's missing wage into a lesson in attitude. I want the younger workers to see skill rewarded without being told hardship proves a failure to try.

headlineQuote: My master electrician's licence doesn't turn another worker's missing wage into a lesson in attitude.
portrait: **Carlos, 43**, is a highly skilled lead with a two-year technical diploma, master electrician's licence and pay above the usual rate.
His **partner** works at a bakery, with two school-age children, a mortgage, fourteen months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
He has **never used AI**, preferring paper evidence and practical teaching while seeking worker involvement before equipment and staffing decisions.
His **public-learning campaign** seeks paid access without claiming an entitlement exists, while model-kit savings remain new deposits conditional on essential bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives less adjustment time before robots around 2031 could affect both adults' physical-work wages.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical learning** and written paid hours would support usable choices.
**Worker involvement** before staffing decisions would help, with access that does not depend on a household already having large savings.
